'''Steven Jay Hatfill''' (born October 24, 1953) is an American [[pathologist]] and [[biological weapon]]s expert. In 2002, he came to worldwide attention as a suspect in the [[2001 anthrax attacks]],<ref name="exonerated">{{cite news|last=Lichtblau|first=Eric|url=https://archive.nytimes.com/www.nytimes.com/2008/08/09/washington/09anthrax.html|title=Scientist Officially Exonerated in Anthrax Attacks|work=The New York Times|date=August 9, 2008|access-date=October 28, 2025}}</ref> a charge of which he was eventually exonerated, and later compensated for, after extensive litigation.

In 2020, Hatfill became an advisor to the [[First presidency of Donald Trump|first Trump White House]], in which capacity he promoted the use of [[hydroxychloroquine]] to treat the [[COVID-19 virus]] despite [[FDA]] objections to the drug. After the 2020 election he participated in{{clarification needed|date=February 2023}} [[Donald Trump]]'s [[Attempts to overturn the 2020 United States presidential election|attempt to overturn the election results]].<ref name = "Diamond"/>

In April 2025, Hatfill became a special advisor to the [[Second presidency of Donald Trump|second Trump administration]] on the subject of pandemic preparedness.<ref name="sun-2025"/> He was fired from the [[Department of Health and Human Services]] on October 27, 2025.<ref name="Stolberg">{{cite news|last=Stolberg|first=Sheryl Gay|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2025/10/28/us/politics/hatfill-covid-hhs-ousted.html|title=Steven Hatfill, Covid Vaccine Critic, Is Ousted From H.H.S.|work=The New York Times|date=October 28, 2025|access-date=October 28, 2025|url-access=limited}}</ref>

==Overview==
Hatfill became the subject of extensive media coverage beginning in mid-2002, when he was a suspect in the [[2001 anthrax attacks]].<ref name="exonerated"/> His home was repeatedly raided by the FBI, his [[Telephone tapping|phone was tapped]], and he was extensively [[Surveillance|surveilled]] for more than two years; he was also terminated from his job at [[Science Applications International Corporation]] (SAIC).<ref name="Freed">{{cite web|first=David|last=Freed|url=http://www.theatlantic.com/magazine/archive/2010/05/the-wrong-man/8019/?single_page=true|title=The Wrong Man|work=The Atlantic|date=May 2010|access-date=October 28, 2025|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110809211317/http://www.theatlantic.com/magazine/archive/2010/05/the-wrong-man/8019/?single_page=true|archive-date=August 9, 2011|url-status=dead|url-access=subscription}}</ref> At a news conference in August 2002, Hatfill denied that he had anything to do with the anthrax letters and said "irresponsible news media coverage based on government [[News leak|leaks]]" had "[[Character assassination|destroyed his reputation]]".<ref name="exonerated"/> He filed a [[lawsuit]] in 2003, accusing the FBI agents and [[United States Department of Justice|Justice Department]] officials who led the criminal investigation of leaking information about him to the press in violation of the [[Privacy Act of 1974|Privacy Act]].<ref name="exonerated"/>

In 2008, the government [[Legal settlement|settled]] Hatfill's lawsuit with a $4.6 million [[annuity]], totalling $5.8 million in payment.<ref name="is paid">{{cite news
|url=https://archive.nytimes.com/www.nytimes.com/2008/06/28/washington/28hatfill.html|title=Scientist Is Paid Millions by U.S. in Anthrax Suit|first1=Scott|last1=Shane|first2=Eric|last2=Lichtblau |work=The New York Times|date=June 28, 2008|access-date=October 28, 2025}}</ref> The government officially exonerated him of any involvement in the anthrax attacks, and the Justice Department identified another military scientist, [[Bruce Edwards Ivins]], as the sole perpetrator of the anthrax attacks.<ref name="exonerated"/> [[Jeffrey A. Taylor]], the [[United States Attorney for the District of Columbia|U.S. Attorney for the District of Columbia]], wrote in a letter to Hatfill's lawyer that "we have concluded, based on laboratory access records, witness accounts and other information, that Dr. Hatfill did not have access to the particular anthrax used in the attacks, and that he was not involved in the anthrax mailings."<ref name="exonerated"/>

In 2004, Hatfill filed lawsuits against several periodicals and journalists who had identified him as a figure warranting further investigation in the anthrax attacks. He sued [[New York Times Company|the New York Times Company]] and ''[[New York Times]]'' columnist [[Nicholas Kristof]] for [[defamation]], [[defamation per se|defamation ''per se'']], and [[intentional infliction of emotional distress]] in connection with five of Kristof's columns in 2002. The courts dismissed this suit, finding that Hatfill was a [[limited purpose public figure|limited-purpose public figure]].<ref>{{cite news|first=Jerry|last=Markon|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/wp-dyn/articles/A47994-2004Jul13.html|title=Former Army Scientist Sues New York Times, Columnist|newspaper=The Washington Post|date=July 14, 2004|access-date=October 28, 2025|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070807215043/https://www.washingtonpost.com/wp-dyn/articles/A47994-2004Jul13.html|archive-date=August 7, 2007|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last=Connor |first=Timothy J. |date=October 2008 |title=Fourth Circuit Throws Out Hatfill Libel Claim Against The New York Times |url=https://www.hklaw.com/publications/Fourth-Circuit-Throws-Out-Hatfill-Libel-Claim-Against-The-New-York-Times-09-03-2008/ |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090107130525/http://www.hklaw.com/id24660/PublicationId2443/ReturnId31/contentid52398/ |archive-date=7 January 2009 |access-date=30 October 2025 |work=Media and Communications Newsletter|publisher=[[Holland & Knight]]}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|first=Bill|last=Mears|url=https://www.cnn.com/2008/US/12/15/anthrax.libel.suit/index.html|title=High court tosses scientist's libel suit against New York Times|publisher=CNN|date=December 15, 2008|access-date=October 28, 2025|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090201041625/http://www.cnn.com/2008/US/12/15/anthrax.libel.suit/index.html|archive-date=February 1, 2009|url-status=dead}}</ref> In 2007, Hatfill settled a similar libel lawsuit against ''[[Vanity Fair (magazine)|Vanity Fair]]'' and ''[[Reader's Digest]]'' for an undisclosed amount, after both magazines agreed to formally retract any implication that Hatfill was involved in the anthrax mailings.<ref>{{Cite web | first=Josh | last=Gerstein | url=http://www.nysun.com/national/hatfill-settles-10m-libel-lawsuit/49333/ | title=Hatfill Settles $10M Libel Lawsuit | work=New York Sun | date=February 27, 2007 | access-date= October 28, 2025| archive-date=June 12, 2008| archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080612102622/http://www.nysun.com/national/hatfill-settles-10m-libel-lawsuit/49333/ | url-status=dead}}</ref>

In 2010, Hatfill was an independent researcher and an adjunct assistant professor of [[emergency medicine]] at the [[George Washington University Medical Center]].<ref name=Bird2014>{{cite magazine|first=Cameron|last=Bird|url=http://www.newsweek.com/2014/06/27/steven-hatfills-strange-trip-accused-terrorist-medical-adventurer-255295.html|title=Steven Hatfill's Strange Trip From Accused Terrorist to Medical Adventurer|magazine=[[Newsweek]]|date=June 18, 2014|access-date=October 30, 2025|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160101213248/http://www.newsweek.com/2014/06/27/steven-hatfills-strange-trip-accused-terrorist-medical-adventurer-255295.html|archive-date=January 1, 2016|url-status=dead}}</ref> He has criticized the response of health authorities to the [[Ebola virus epidemic in West Africa]] and suggested that it is possible that Ebola could be [[Ebola#Transmission|transmitted]] by [[aerosol]], a position which other experts have criticized.<ref name="21 days">{{cite magazine|first=James|last=Hamblin|url=https://www.theatlantic.com/health/archive/2014/10/21-days/381901/?single_page=true|title=21 Days|magazine=[[The Atlantic]]|date=October 26, 2014|access-date=October 28, 2025|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150131141040/https://www.theatlantic.com/health/archive/2014/10/21-days/381901/?single_page=true|archive-date=January 31, 2015|url-access=subscription|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref name="assessing the">{{cite magazine|first=Stephen|last=Goldstein|url=http://www.theatlantic.com/health/archive/2014/10/clarity-in-ebola-transmission-science/382026/?single_page=true|title=Assessing the Science of Ebola Transmission|magazine=[[The Atlantic]]|date=October 28, 2014|access-date=October 28, 2025|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141206000400/http://www.theatlantic.com/health/archive/2014/10/clarity-in-ebola-transmission-science/382026/?single_page=true|archive-date=December 6, 2014|url-status=dead|url-access=subscription}}</ref>

==Early life==
Hatfill was born in [[St. Louis, Missouri]], and graduated from [[Mattoon High School|Mattoon Senior High School]], [[Mattoon, Illinois]] (1971), and [[Southwestern College (Kansas)|Southwestern College]] in [[Winfield, Kansas]] (1975), where he studied [[biology]].

Hatfill was enlisted as a [[private (rank)|private]] in the [[U.S. Army]] from 1975 to 1977.<ref name="Cooper 2003">Cooper, Simon. "The Lesson of Steve Hatfill", [[Seed (magazine)|''Seed'' magazine]], May/June 2003.</ref>{{page needed|date=October 2025}} (In 1999, during an interview with a journalist, he claimed to have been a "captain in the [[U.S. Army Special Forces|U.S. Special Forces]]", but a subsequent investigation revealed that, according to the Army, he had never served with the Special Forces.<ref>[[Richard Preston|Preston, Richard]] (2002), ''[[The Demon in the Freezer]]'', New York: Random House, pp. 206–07.</ref>) Following his Army discharge, Hatfill qualified and worked as a [[Medical Laboratory Scientist|medical laboratory technician]], but soon resolved to become a doctor. He worked as a medical missionary in Kapanga, Zaire, under a mentor, Dr. [[Glenn Eschtruth]], who was murdered there in 1977. A brief marriage, from 1976 to 1978, to Eschtruth's daughter, Caroline Ruth Eschtruth, produced one daughter.

==Medical education==
In 1978, Hatfill settled in [[Rhodesia]] (now [[Zimbabwe]]) and entered the [[Godfrey Huggins Medical School]]<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.btinternet.com/~zimdocs/index.html |title=Zimbabwe Medical Graduates Worldwide |access-date=January 31, 2007 |url-status=unfit |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100814031026/http://www.btinternet.com/~zimdocs/index.html |archive-date=August 14, 2010}}</ref> at the [[University of Rhodesia]] in Salisbury (now [[Harare]]). (His claimed military associations during this period included assistance as a medic with the [[Selous Scouts]] and membership in the [[C Squadron 22 (Rhodesian) SAS|Rhodesian SAS]], but according to one journalist<ref name="Cooper 2003"/>{{page needed|date=October 2025}} the regimental association of the latter is "adamant Hatfill never belonged to the unit".) After failing in 1983, he graduated in 1984 with an [[Bachelor of Medicine, Bachelor of Surgery|MB ChB]] degree and, from 1984 to 1985, completed a one-year [[medical internship|internship]] at a small rural hospital in [[South Africa]]'s [[North West (South African province)|North West Province]]. The South African government recruited him to be a medical officer on a 14-month tour of duty, from 1986 to 1988, in Antarctica with the [[South African National Antarctic Expedition]] (SANAE). In 1988, he completed a [[master's degree]] in [[microbiology]] at the [[University of Cape Town]]. Two years later, he worked toward a second master's degree—in medical biochemistry and radiation biology—at the [[University of Stellenbosch]], while employed as a medical technician in the university's clinical haematology lab. A three-year [[Hematology|haematological pathology]] residency at Stellenbosch from 1991 to 1993 followed. Hatfill also conducted research toward a Ph.D. between 1992 and 1995—under the supervision of microbiology professor Ralph Kirby at [[Rhodes University]]—on the treatment of [[leukemia]] with [[thalidomide]].<ref name="Cooper 2003"/>{{page needed|date=October 2025}}

Hatfill submitted his Ph.D. thesis for examination to Rhodes University in January 1995, but it failed in November.<ref name="Cooper 2003"/>{{page needed|date=October 2025}} Hatfill later claimed to have completed a Ph.D. degree in "[[molecular cell biology]]" at Rhodes, as well as a post-doctoral fellowship (1994–95) at the [[University of Oxford]] in [[England]] and three [[master's degree]]s (in [[microbial genetics]], [[biochemistry|medical biochemistry]], and [[experimental pathology]], respectively). Some of these credentials have been seriously questioned or disputed. During a later investigation, officials at Rhodes maintained that their institution had never awarded him a Ph.D.<ref>Preston, ''Op. cit.'', pp. 207–08.</ref> In 2007, Hatfill's lawyer Tom Connolly<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.hwglaw.com/team/thomas-g-connolly/ |title=Thomas G. Connolly}}</ref> – in his lawsuit against former U.S. Attorney General [[John Ashcroft]] and the [[FBI]] – admitted that his client had "[p]uffed on his resume," falsely claiming he had earned a PhD and had "[f]orged a diploma" for the PhD.<ref name="cbsnews">{{Cite web|url=http://www.cbsnews.com/stories/2007/03/09/60minutes/main2552906.shtml|title=Tables Turned In Anthrax Probe|website=60 Minutes|publisher=CBS News|date=March 9, 2007|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070314201834/http://www.cbsnews.com/stories/2007/03/09/60minutes/main2552906.shtml|archive-date=March 14, 2007|access-date=October 29, 2025|url-status=dead|pages=[https://web.archive.org/web/20070314201834/http://www.cbsnews.com/stories/2007/03/09/60minutes/main2552906.shtml 1], [https://web.archive.org/web/20070315012456/http://www.cbsnews.com/stories/2007/03/09/60minutes/main2552906_page2.shtml 2], [https://web.archive.org/web/20070315012518/http://www.cbsnews.com/stories/2007/03/09/60minutes/main2552906_page4.shtml 4]}}</ref>{{rp|4}}

Back in the United States, another of Hatfill's post-doctoral appointments commenced at the [[National Institute of Child Health and Human Development]] (NICHD), one of the [[National Institutes of Health]] (NIH) in [[Bethesda, Maryland]], in 1995. He then worked from 1997 to 1999 as a civilian researcher at the [[United States Army Medical Research Institute of Infectious Diseases]] (USAMRIID), the [[United States Department of Defense|U.S. Department of Defense]]'s medical research institute for [[biological warfare]] (BW) defense at [[Fort Detrick]], Frederick, [[Maryland]]. There, he studied, under a [[United States National Research Council|National Research Council]] fellowship, new drug treatments for the [[Ebola virus]] and became an authority on BW defense.

==Anthrax attacks==
In January 1999, Hatfill transferred to a "consulting job" at [[Science Applications International Corporation]] (SAIC), which has a "sprawling campus" in nearby [[McLean, Virginia]]. The corporation worked for a multitude of federal agencies. Many projects were [[classified information|classified]]. Hatfill designed BW defense training curricula for government agencies.

By this time, there had been several [[anthrax hoaxes|hoax anthrax mailings]] in the United States. Hatfill and his collaborator, SAIC vice president Joseph Soukup, commissioned [[William C. Patrick]], retired head of the old US bioweapons program (who had also been a mentor of Hatfill), to write a report on the possibilities of terrorist anthrax mailing attacks. [[Barbara Hatch Rosenberg]] (director of the [[Federation of American Scientists]]' biochem weapons working group in 2002) said that the report was commissioned "under a [[CIA]] contract to SAIC".  But SAIC said Hatfill and Soukup had commissioned it {{nowrap|internally{{snd}}}} there was no outside client.

The resulting report, dated February 1999, was subsequently seen by some as a "blueprint" for the [[2001 anthrax attacks]].  Amongst other things, it suggested the maximum amount of anthrax {{nowrap|powder{{snd}}}}{{nowrap|2.5 grams{{snd}}}} that could be put in an envelope without making a suspicious bulge.  The quantity in the envelope sent to Senator [[Patrick Leahy]] in October 2001 was 0.871&nbsp;grams.<ref>{{cite news| url=https://archive.nytimes.com/www.nytimes.com/2002/05/07/national/07ANTH.html| work=The New York Times | title=Anthrax Sent Through Mail Gained Potency by the Letter | first1=William J. | last1=Broad | first2=David | last2=Johnston | date=May 7, 2002|access-date=October 28, 2025}}</ref>  After the attacks, the report drew the attention of the media and others and led to their investigation of Patrick and Hatfill.<ref>{{cite web|first=William J.|last=Broad|url=https://archive.nytimes.com/www.nytimes.com/2001/12/03/national/03POWD.html|title=Terror Anthrax Linked to Type Made by U.S.|work=The New York Times|date=December 3, 2001|access-date=October 30, 2025}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|first1=Guy|last1=Gugliotta |first2= Dan|last2= Eggen|url=http://www.ph.ucla.edu/EPI/bioter/biowarfareexpertsques.html|title=Biological Warfare Experts Questioned in Anthrax Probe|newspaper=The Washington Post|date=June 28, 2002 |access-date=October 30, 2025|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20020812130807/http://www.ph.ucla.edu/EPI/bioter/biowarfareexpertsques.html|archive-date=August 12, 2002|url-status=dead|via=UCLA}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|last=Ross|first=Brian|url=http://abcnews.go.com/sections/wnt/DailyNews/anthrax020627.html|title=Blueprint for Anthrax Attack|publisher=ABC News|work=World News Tonight with Peter Jennings|date=June 27, 2002|access-date=October 30, 2025|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20021010003328/http://abcnews.go.com/sections/wnt/DailyNews/anthrax020627.html|archive-date=October 10, 2002|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref name=Thompson2003>{{cite news|first=Marilyn W.|last=Thompson|url=http://www.washingtonpost.com/ac2/wp-dyn/A49717-2003Sep9|title=The Pursuit of Steven Hatfill|newspaper=The Washington Post|date=September 9, 2003|page=W06|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111018025455/http://www.washingtonpost.com/ac2/wp-dyn/A49717-2003Sep9|archive-date=October 18, 2011|url-status=dead|access-date=October 30, 2025}}</ref>

===Assertions by Rosenberg===

As soon as it became known, in October 2001, that the [[Ames strain]] of anthrax had been used in the attacks, Barbara Hatch Rosenberg and others began suggesting that the mailings might be the work of a "rogue CIA agent" and they provided the name of the "most likely" person to the FBI. On November 21, 2001, Rosenberg made similar statements to the Biological and Toxic Weapons convention in Geneva.<ref>{{Cite journal |doi = 10.1126/science.297.5585.1264|pmid = 12193766|title = PROFILE: BARBARA HATCH ROSENBERG: Unconventional Detective Bears Down on a Killer|journal = Science|volume = 297|issue = 5585|pages = 1264–1265|year = 2002|last1 = Couzin|first1 = J.|s2cid = 176721295}}</ref>  In December 2001, she published "A Compilation of Evidence and Comments on the Source of the Mailed Anthrax" via the website of the [[Federation of American Scientists]] (FAS) suggesting the attacks were "perpetrated with the unwitting assistance of a sophisticated government program".<ref>{{Cite web | url=http://www.ph.ucla.edu/epi/bioter/compilationofanthraxevidence.html |title = A Compilation of Evidence and Comments on the Source of the Mailed Anthrax|last=Rosenberg|first=Barbara Hatch|date=December 10, 2001|access-date=October 30, 2025|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20050913135118/http://www.ph.ucla.edu/epi/bioter/compilationofanthraxevidence.html|archive-date=September 13, 2005|url-status=dead|publisher=UCLA}}</ref>

Rosenberg discussed the case with reporters from the ''New York Times''.<ref>{{cite news | url=https://archive.nytimes.com/www.nytimes.com/2001/12/14/national/14ANTH.html | work=The New York Times | title=F.B.I. Queries Expert Who Sees Federal Lab Tie in Anthrax Cases | first=William J. | last=Broad | date=December 14, 2001 | access-date=October 30, 2025 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20020209014025/http://www10.nytimes.com/2001/12/14/national/14ANTH.html | archive-date=February 9, 2002 | url-status=live }}</ref>  On January 4, 2002, [[Nicholas Kristof]] of the ''New York Times'' published a column titled "Profile of a Killer"<ref name="nytimes.com">{{cite news| url=https://archive.nytimes.com/www.nytimes.com/2002/01/04/opinion/04KRIS.html | work=The New York Times | title=Profile of a Killer | first=Nicholas D. | last=Kristof | date=January 4, 2002|access-date=October 28, 2025}}</ref> stating, "I think I know who sent out the anthrax last fall."  For months, Rosenberg gave speeches and stated her beliefs to many reporters from around the world.  She posted "Analysis of the Anthrax Attacks" to the FAS website on January 17, 2002.  On February 5, 2002, she published an article called "Is the FBI Dragging Its Feet?"<ref>{{Cite magazine|last=Lemann|first=Nicholas | url=http://www.newyorker.com/archive/2002/03/18/020318ta_talk_lemann |title = The Anthrax Culprit|magazine = The New Yorker|date = March 18, 2002|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070815203213/http://www.newyorker.com/archive/2002/03/18/020318ta_talk_lemann|archive-date=August 15, 2007|url-status=dead|url-access=subscription}}</ref>  At the time, the FBI denied reports that investigators had identified a chief suspect, saying, "There is no prime suspect in this case at this time."<ref>{{cite news| url=https://archive.nytimes.com/www.nytimes.com/2002/02/26/national/26ANTH.html| work=The New York Times | title=U.S. Says Short List of 'Suspects' Is Being Checked in Anthrax Case | first1=Judith | last1=Miller | first2=William J. | last2=Broad | date=February 26, 2002|access-date=October 28, 2025}}</ref>  ''The Washington Post'' reported that "FBI officials over the last week have flatly discounted Dr. Rosenberg's claims."<ref>{{Cite news | url=http://www.ph.ucla.edu/epi/bioter/FBIlackssuspect.html | last1=Eggen|first1=Dan|last2=Warrick|first2=Joby|title=FBI Still Lacks Identifiable Suspect in Anthrax Probe|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20030101181030/http://www.ph.ucla.edu/epi/bioter/FBIlackssuspect.html|archive-date=January 1, 2003|url-status=dead|newspaper=The Washington Post|date=February 26, 2002|access-date=October 28, 2025|via=UCLA}}</ref>

On June 13, 2002, Rosenberg posted "The Anthrax Case: What the FBI Knows" to the FAS site. Five days later, Rosenberg presented her theories to Senate staffers working for Senators Daschle and Leahy.<ref name="dir.salon.com">{{cite web |last=York|first=Anthony|url=https://www.salon.com/2002/06/21/rosenberg_4/ |title=I'm ready for my close-up, Sen. Daschle |work=[[Salon (website)|Salon]] |access-date=October 28, 2025 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060615235317/http://dir.salon.com/story/politics/feature/2002/06/21/rosenberg/index.html |archive-date=June 15, 2006}}</ref>  On June 25, the FBI publicly searched Hatfill's apartment, turning him into a household name. "The FBI also pointed out that Hatfill had agreed to the search and is not considered a suspect."<ref>{{cite news|author1=Dave Altimari |author2=Jack Dolan |author3=David Lightman  |name-list-style=amp |title= The Case Of Dr. Hatfill: Suspect Or Pawn|url=http://www.ctnow.com/news/custom/newsat3/hc-anthrax0627.artjun27,0,4961407.story?coll=hc-headlines-newsat3|newspaper=Hartford Courant|date=June 27, 2002|access-date=October 28, 2025|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20021221043804/http://www.ctnow.com/news/custom/newsat3/hc-anthrax0627.artjun27,0,4961407.story?coll=hc-headlines-newsat3|archive-date=December 21, 2002|url-status=dead}}</ref> ''[[The American Prospect]]'' reported in June 2002: "Hatfill is not a suspect in the anthrax case, the FBI says."<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Rozen|first=Laura|url =http://www.prospect.org/webfeatures/2002/06/rozen-l-06-27.html|title = Who is Steven Hatfill?|journal = The American Prospect|date = June 27, 2002|access-date = October 30, 2025|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20021013182423/http://www.prospect.org/webfeatures/2002/06/rozen-l-06-27.html|archive-date=October 13, 2002|url-status=dead}}</ref>  On August 3, 2002, Rosenberg told the media that the FBI had asked her if "a team of government scientists could be trying to frame Steven J. Hatfill."<ref>{{Cite web | url=http://www.washtimes.com/metro/20020803-26337484.htm|title = Scientist Says FBI Asked about Setup|work=The Washington Times|last=Taylor|first=Guy|date=August 3, 2002|access-date=October 30, 2025|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20020806183042/http://www.washtimes.com/metro/20020803-26337484.htm|archive-date=August 6, 2002|url-status=dead}}</ref>

===Person of interest===
In August 2002, U.S. Attorney General [[John Ashcroft]] labelled Hatfill a "[[person of interest]]" in a press conference, although no charges were brought against him. Hatfill, who researched viruses, vehemently denied having any connection to the anthrax mailings and sued the FBI, the Justice Department, John Ashcroft, [[Alberto Gonzales]], and others for violating his constitutional rights and the [[Privacy Act of 1974|Privacy Act]]. On June 27, 2008, the Department of Justice announced it would settle Hatfill's case for $5.8&nbsp;million.<ref name="is paid"/>

Hatfill later went to work at [[Pennington Biomedical Research Center]] in [[Baton Rouge]], [[Louisiana]]. In September 2001, SAIC was commissioned by the Pentagon to create a replica of a mobile WMD "laboratory", alleged to have been used by [[Saddam Hussein]], then President of Iraq. The Pentagon said the trailer was to be used as a training aid for teams seeking weapons of mass destruction in Iraq.<ref>{{cite news|first1=William J. |last1=Broad|first2=David|last2=Johnston|url=https://archive.nytimes.com/www.nytimes.com/2003/07/02/national/02GERM.html|title=ASubject of Anthrax Inquiry Tied to Anti-Germ Training|work=The New York Times|date=July 2, 2003|access-date=October 28, 2025}}</ref>

His lawyer, Victor M. Glasberg, stated: "Steve's life has been devastated by a drumbeat of innuendo, implication and speculation. We have a frightening public attack on an individual who, guilty or not, should not be exposed to this type of public opprobrium based on speculation."<ref>{{Cite news|url=http://www.ph.ucla.edu/epi/bioter/scientistsdeniesroleanthrax.html|title=Ex-Army Scientist Denies Role in Anthrax Attacks|newspaper=[[The Washington Post]] |via=ph.ucla.edu |date=August 11, 2002 |first=Tom |last=Jackman|access-date=October 30, 2025|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20020830171613/http://www.ph.ucla.edu/epi/bioter/scientistsdeniesroleanthrax.html|archive-date=August 30, 2002|url-status=dead}}</ref>

In an embarrassing incident, FBI agents trailing Hatfill in a motor vehicle ran over his foot when he attempted to approach them in May 2003. Police responding to the incident did not cite the driver, but issued Hatfill a citation for "walking to create a hazard".<ref>{{Cite web|first=Kelli|last=Arena|url=http://www.cnn.com/2003/US/05/19/hatfill/|title=Hatfill ticketed in altercation with FBI agent|date=May 19, 2003|publisher=CNN|access-date=October 30, 2025|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20031009154758/http://www.cnn.com/2003/US/05/19/hatfill/|archive-date=October 9, 2003|url-status=dead}}</ref> He and his attorneys fought the ticket, but a hearing officer upheld the ticket and ordered Hatfill to pay the requisite $5 fine.<ref>{{Cite news|last=Cauvin|first=Henri E.|url=http://www.ph.ucla.edu/epi/Bioter/scientistround.html|title=Scientist Loses Latest Round|newspaper=The Washington Post|date=August 16, 2003|access-date=October 30, 2025|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20030914035522/http://www.ph.ucla.edu/epi/Bioter/scientistround.html|archive-date=September 14, 2003|url-status=dead|via=UCLA}}</ref>

FBI Director [[Robert Mueller]] changed leadership of the investigation in late 2006, and at that time, another suspect, [[USAMRIID]] bacteriologist [[Bruce Ivins]], became the main focus of the investigation.<ref name="lat">{{cite news |url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-2008-aug-01-na-anthrax1-story.html|title=Apparent suicide in anthrax case |first=David |last=Willman |work=[[Los Angeles Times]] |date=August 1, 2008 |access-date=October 30, 2025|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080805071256/http://www.latimes.com/news/nationworld/nation/la-na-anthrax1-2008aug01,0,4086498,full.story|archive-date=August 5, 2008|url-status=dead|url-access=limited}}</ref>
Considerable questions were raised about the credibility of the case against Ivins, as well.<ref>{{cite news|first=Allan|last=Lengel|url=http://www.aolnews.com/nation/article/some-doubt-fbis-findings-that-scientist-bruce-ivins-sent-anthrax-letters/19372388|title=Some Doubt FBI Line That Scientist Sent Anthrax Letters|publisher=[[AOL News]]|date=February 25, 2010|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100227010238/http://www.aolnews.com/nation/article/some-doubt-fbis-findings-that-scientist-bruce-ivins-sent-anthrax-letters/19372388|archive-date=February 27, 2010|access-date=October 30, 2025}}</ref>

===''60 Minutes'' interview===
Hatfill's lawyer, Tom Connolly, was featured in a ''[[60 Minutes]]'' interview about the anthrax incidents on March 11, 2007.<ref name="cbsnews"/>{{rp|1}} In the interview, Connolly revealed that Hatfill faked his Ph.D. degree: "It is true. He has indeed puffed on his resume. Absolutely. Forged a diploma. Yes, that's true." He went on to state, "Listen, if puffing on your resume made you the anthrax killer, then half this town should be suspects."

''[[The Washington Post Magazine]]'' stated in 2003 that Hatfill had obtained an anti-anthrax medicine ([[ciprofloxacin]], which is an [[antibiotic]] medication) immediately before the anthrax mailings.<ref name=Thompson2003 /> Connolly explained to ''60 Minutes'', "Before the attacks, he had surgery. So yes, he's on [[Cipro]]. But the fuller truth is, in fact he was on Cipro because a doctor gave it to him after sinus surgery."<ref name="cbsnews"/>{{rp|2}} Hatfill had previously said the antibiotic was for a lingering sinus infection.<ref name=Thompson2003 />  The omission in the ''Times''' article of the reason why he had been taking Cipro is one reason Hatfill sued the newspaper. The newspaper won a summary judgment ruling in early 2007, squelching the libel suit that had been filed by Steven Hatfill against it and columnist [[Nicholas Kristof]].<ref name=autogenerated1>{{Cite web |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070930204409/http://www.law.com/jsp/ihc/PubArticleIHC.jsp?id=1177059862981 |archive-date=September 30, 2007 |url=http://www.law.com/jsp/ihc/PubArticleIHC.jsp?id=1177059862981|title=Newspaper of Record Involved in Extraordinary Cases |website=[[National Law Journal]] |first=Roger |last=Adler |via=law.com |date=April 23, 2007}}</ref>

==Lawsuits==
===''Hatfill v. John Ashcroft, et al.''===
In August 2003, Hatfill sued [[Attorney General of the United States|U.S. Attorney General]] [[John Ashcroft]], the [[United States Department of Justice|U.S. Department of Justice]], the [[Federal Bureau of Investigation|FBI]], FBI Supervisory Special Agent Van Harp, two DOJ employees, and an unknown number of FBI agents, alleging that the government denied his constitutional rights and attempted to scapegoat him for the anthrax attacks. The suit was filed in the [[U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia]].<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://fl1.findlaw.com/news.findlaw.com/cnn/docs/hatfill/hatfillash82603cmp.pdf |title=''Steven J. Hatfill, M.D. v. Attorney General John Ashcroft'' |access-date=2007-03-14 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070221113509/http://fl1.findlaw.com/news.findlaw.com/cnn/docs/hatfill/hatfillash82603cmp.pdf |archive-date=2007-02-21 |url-status=dead}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.cnn.com/2003/LAW/08/26/lawsuit.hatfill/index.html |title=Anthrax 'person of interest' sues Ashcroft, FBI |date=August 27, 2003|publisher=CNN|access-date=October 30, 2025|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20040206025715/http://www.cnn.com/2003/LAW/08/26/lawsuit.hatfill/index.html|archive-date=February 6, 2004|url-status=dead}}</ref>

In March 2007, U.S. District Judge [[Reggie Walton]] allowed Hatfill to re-[[subpoena]] various reporters, seeking the names of government sources who had told reporters that Hatfill was under investigation. During an earlier round of [[discovery (law)|discovery]], Hatfill issued subpoenas to six reporters ([[Michael Isikoff]] and Daniel Klaidman of ''[[Newsweek]]'', [[Brian Ross (journalist)|Brian Ross]] of [[ABC News (United States)|ABC]], Allan Lengel of ''[[The Washington Post]]'', Jim Stewart of [[CBS News|CBS]], and Toni Locy of ''[[USA Today]]'').<ref name=Schwartz2007>{{Cite web|url=https://legaltimes.typepad.com/blt/2007/05/the_medias_stra.html |first=Emma |last=Schwartz |date=May 1, 2007 |title=The Media's Strange Ally|website=The BLT: The Blog of Legal Times|access-date=October 30, 2025|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070927105534/https://legaltimes.typepad.com/blt/2007/05/the_medias_stra.html|archive-date=September 27, 2007|url-status=dead}}</ref> In the second round of subpoenas, Hatfill subpoenaed eight news outlets, including three not previously subpoenaed. The federal government opposed Hatfill's move as an impermissible expansion of discovery.<ref name=Schwartz2007/><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://pdfserver.amlaw.com/dc/hatfill_DOJ.pdf|title=DOJ's Motion}}</ref>

In March 2008, Walton held Toni Locy of ''USA Today'' in [[contempt of court]] for declining to identify her sources, fining her $500 per day, escalating to $5,000 a day, until she identified her sources.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.usatoday.com/news/washington/2008-03-07-anthrax-reporter_N.htm|title=Reporter held in contempt for anthrax case|last=Johnson|first=Kevin|date=March 7, 2008|work=USA Today|access-date=October 30, 2025|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080312072735/http://www.usatoday.com/news/washington/2008-03-07-anthrax-reporter_N.htm|archive-date=March 12, 2008|url-status=dead}}</ref> On appeal, the [[U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit]] suspended the fines against Locy,<ref name=RSF2008>[https://rsf.org/en/last-minute-decision-appeal-court-suspends-fines-journalist-refusing-name-sources Last-minute decision by appeal court suspends fines for journalist refusing to name sources], Reporters Without Borders (2008).</ref> and in November 2008 threw out the order because the case had settled.<ref>{{cite web|last=Tschiggfrie|first=Sarah|title=Locy Contempt Citation Overturned|url=https://columns.wlu.edu/locy-contempt-citation-overturned/|work=The Columns|publisher=Washington & Lee University|date=November 21, 2008|access-date=October 30, 2025}}</ref> Locy's position was supported by the [[Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press]] and [[Reporters Without Borders]]<ref name=RSF2008/> and she received the [[National Press Club (USA)|National Press Club]]'s John Aubuchon Freedom of the Press Award for her stance.<ref>Sarah Tschiggfrie, [https://columns.wlu.edu/journalism-professor-toni-locy-receives-press-freedom-award/ Journalism Professor Toni Locy Receives Press Freedom Award] (July 18, 2008).</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.rcfp.org/locy-appeal-dismissed-contempt-order-vacated/|title=Locy appeal dismissed, contempt order vacated|publisher=Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press|date=November 17, 2008|access-date=October 30, 2025}}</ref>

In January 2008, Walton ordered the parties to attempt [[mediation]], and set a tentative trial date of December 2008 if settlement talks failed.<ref>{{Cite news|url=http://www.latimes.com/news/nationworld/nation/la-na-anthrax12jan12,0,646463.story|title=U.S. attorney's office accused of anthrax case leaks|last=Willman|first=David|date=January 12, 2008|newspaper=Los Angeles Times|access-date=October 30, 2025|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080115063703/http://www.latimes.com/news/nationworld/nation/la-na-anthrax12jan12,0,646463.story?|archive-date=January 15, 2008|url-status=dead|url-access=limited}}</ref> In June 2008, a settlement was announced, in which the Justice Department agreed to pay $4.6 million (consisting of $2.825 million in cash and an annuity paying $150,000 a year for 20 years) to Hatfill. The settlement did not include an admission of  liability by the government.<ref name="is paid"/>

===''Hatfill v. The New York Times''===
In June 2003, Hatfill sued [[The New York Times Company]] and [[Nicholas D. Kristof]] for defamation in Virginia state court.<ref name=2005FourthCir>''[https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=14375647997211492969 Hatfill v. New York Times Co.]'', 416 F.3d 320 (4th Cir. 2005).</ref> Hatfill alleged that Kristof had published columns implying that he was responsible for the anthrax mailings, and thus defamed him.<ref name=2005FourthCir/> He refiled the suit in federal court in July 2004, alleging defamation and [[intentional infliction of emotional distress]].<ref name=2005FourthCir/> After filing his complaint, Hatfill voluntarily dropped Kristof as a defendant because the federal district court lacked [[personal jurisdiction]] over the columnist.<ref name=2005FourthCir/>

The federal district court initially granted the newspaper's [[motion to dismiss]], holding that the language in Kristof's columns could not reasonably read as accusing Hatfill of responsibility for anthrax attacks, and that the columns reported information on the federal investigation into Hatfill, without accusing him of guilt.<ref name=2005FourthCir/> The [[U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit]], in July 2005, reversed this ruling (holding that "Kristof's columns, taken together, are capable of defamatory meaning under Virginia law") and returned the case to the district court for further proceedings.<ref name=2005FourthCir/>

In January 2007, Judge [[Claude M. Hilton]] threw out Hatfill's defamation suit against ''The New York Times'', granting [[summary judgment]] to the newspaper.<ref>{{cite web|first=Neil A.|last=Lewis|url=https://archive.nytimes.com/www.nytimes.com/2007/01/13/us/13hatfill.html|title=Judge Rejects Defamation Suit Against The Times|work=The New York Times|date=January 13, 2007|access-date=October 30, 2025|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150605045041/http://www.nytimes.com/2007/01/13/us/13hatfill.html|archive-date=June 5, 2015|url-status=live}}</ref><ref name=2007EDVA>''[https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=123489761777543949 Hatfill v. New York Times Co.]'', 488 F. Supp. 2d 522 (E.D. Va. 2007).</ref> The court held that Hatfill was either a "[[public figure]]" or "public official" and thus could only prevail in a defamation suit if the defendants acted with [[actual malice]], and that Hatfill could not demonstrate that Kristof had acted with actual malice.<ref name=2007EDVA/> The court additionally found that Hatfill could not, [[Judgment as a matter of law|as a matter of law]], meet his [[burden of proof (law)|burden of proof]] that the allegedly defamatory statements were materially false; it also threw out his claim for intentional infliction of emotional distress.<ref name=2007EDVA/>

In July 2008, the Fourth Circuit, in a unanimous decision, affirmed the district court's ruling.<ref name=StoutDecember2008>{{cite news|author=David Stout|url=https://archive.nytimes.com/www.nytimes.com/2008/12/15/washington/15web-hatfill.html|title=Justices Reject Appeal in Anthrax Libel Suit|newspaper=New York Times|date=December 15, 2008|access-date=October 30, 2025|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161107073812/http://www.nytimes.com/2008/12/15/washington/15web-hatfill.html|archive-date=November 7, 2016|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>''[https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=6123587589719331187 Hatfill v. The New York Times Co.]'', 532 F. 3d 312 (4th Cir. 2008).</ref> In December 2008, the Supreme Court [[Certiorari|declined to hear an appeal]], leaving the newspaper's win intact.<ref name=StoutDecember2008/>

===''Hatfill v. Foster''===
[[Donald Wayne Foster]], an expert in [[forensic linguistics]] and a professor at [[Vassar College]], advised the FBI during the investigation of the anthrax attacks. He later wrote an article for ''[[Vanity Fair magazine|Vanity Fair]]'' about his investigation of Hatfill. In the October 2003 article (entitled ""The Message in the Anthrax"), Foster described how he had tried to match up Hatfill's travels with the postmarks on the anthrax letters, and analyzed old interviews and an unpublished novel by Hatfill about a bioterror attack on the United States. Foster wrote that "When I lined up Hatfill's known movements with the postmark locations of reported biothreats, those hoax anthrax attacks appeared to trail him like a vapor cloud."<ref name=Popkin>{{cite web|first=Jim |last=Popkin|url=http://www.msnbc.msn.com/id/6152515/|title=Hatfill strikes back in anthrax case|publisher=NBC News|date=October 4, 2004|access-date=October 30, 2025|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20041012115312/http://www.msnbc.msn.com/id/6152515/|archive-date=October 12, 2004|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref name=VanityFairSettlement>[https://www.rcfp.org/hatfill-settles-vanity-fair/ Hatfill settles with Vanity Fair], Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press (February 26, 2007).</ref>

In 2004, Hatfill sued Foster and [[Condé Nast Publications]], alleging [[defamation]].<ref name=Popkin/> He also sued [[The Reader's Digest Association]] (which had published a condensed version of the article&mdash;entitled "Tracking The Anthrax Killer"&mdash;in the December 2003 issue of ''[[Reader's Digest]]'').<ref name=VanityFairSettlement/> In 2007, the defendants settled the case before trial on undisclosed terms.<ref>{{Cite web|first=Josh|last= Gerstein|url=http://www.nysun.com/article/49333|title=Hatfill Settles $10M Libel Lawsuit|website=The New York Sun|date=February 26, 2007|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070313191558/http://www.nysun.com/article/49333|archive-date=March 13, 2007|url-status=dead|access-date=October 30, 2025}}</ref> A statement by ''Vanity Fair'' issued after the settlement was announced read: "To the extent any statements contained in the article might be read to convey that Condé Nast and Professor Foster were accusing Dr. Hatfill of perpetrating these attacks, Condé Nast and Professor Foster retract any such implication."<ref name=VanityFairSettlement/>

===Hatfill case against blogger===
Hatfill obtained from [[Google]] the [[IP address]] behind the blog of one "Luigi Warren" hosted by Google's [[Blogspot]] web-hosting service. According to ''[[Newsweek]]'', "Luigi Warren" had "operated a lurid rumor mill about Hatfill for more than a decade–promoting, in particular, hearsay about the years he lived and worked in southern Africa during the throes of [[apartheid]]."<ref name=Bird2014 /> In 2010, Hatfill's attorneys sent a letter to a stem-cell research scientist at [[Harvard Medical School]] whom they accused of authoring the "Luigi Warren" posts.<ref name=Bird2014/> The Harvard researcher, however, did not make the posts in question, and instead maintained a different blog, in which he wrote that "the campaign to promote Steven Hatfill as a 'person of interest' ... was a bureaucratic ruse or diversion to maintain a useful [[strategic ambiguity]]."<ref name=Bird2014/> The Harvard researcher believed that someone was impersonating him.<ref name=Bird2014/> Google revealed the IP address for the blog, which was traced to a computer at [[Stellenbosch University]] in South Africa (Hatfill's alma mater); the university identified a [[radiation oncologist]] as the user of the computer in question, and the blogger later agreed to an undisclosed settlement.<ref name=Bird2014/>

==Post-settlement life==
===2010s===
Since the settlements of his legal cases, which included receiving $5.8 million (less legal costs) from the Justice Department (2008) and undisclosed sums from Condé Nast (2008) and the South African medical researcher (2010), Hatfill has pursued activities as an independent researcher. He was appointed an adjunct assistant professor of [[emergency medicine]] at the [[George Washington University Medical Center]] in 2010.<ref name=Bird2014 /> In 2011, he added additional affiliations at GW in "Clinical Research and Leadership" and "Microbiology, Immunology, and Tropical Medicine".<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://smhs.gwu.edu/microbiology/faculty/joint|title=Joint Appointment &#124; The Department of Microbiology, Immunology, & Tropical Medicine|website=smhs.gwu.edu|access-date=December 15, 2019|archive-date=January 3, 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200103151913/https://smhs.gwu.edu/microbiology/faculty/joint|url-status=dead}}</ref> (His BA degree and one MS degree — but not his other previously claimed medical degrees — appear on the GW Faculty Directory.<ref>[https://www.gwumc.edu/smhs/facultydirectory/profile.cfm?empName=Steven%20Hatfill&FacID=2055493436&show=1 "Steven Hatfill"], GW School of Medicine & Health Sciences Faculty Directory. Accessed October 22, 2019.</ref>) He oversaw construction of a "state-of-the-art boat" on which to conduct his own scientific trials. He has allocated more than $1 million of his own money to construct a full-scale prototype of what he calls ''Beagle III''. This craft, with a crew of military veterans and scientists, would ply the waters of "high-biodiversity areas" – the Amazon, or the great rivers of Borneo – seeking and studying rare plants and fungi as sources of new drugs.  A ''Newsweek'' interviewer has described ... <blockquote>...Hatfill's unbuilt, twin-diesel-powered boat. Inside the vessel's aluminum hull, he envisioned a plexus of laboratories, with DNA microarrays and other "space-age zuzu" for analyzing the genetic compositions of plants. Bedrooms would be equipped with video-conferencing systems and DVD players, and the executive cabin was modeled after the president's quarters on [[Air Force One]]...Hatfill had also thrown in a roof-mounted [[cosmic ray]] detector, which would switch on near the equator to capture data on "high-energy cosmic ray showers". An onboard chef from the ranks of [[Le Cordon Bleu]] would fuel a crew of scientists and trainees, and a 30-day supply of dehydrated food would hedge against disaster.<ref name=Bird2014 /></blockquote>
 
Hatfill owns a colonial-style brick home in [[Marion County, Florida]] as well as a property in the [[El Yunque National Forest|El Yunque]] rain forest, in [[Puerto Rico]], where he has run a military-style [[Outward Bound]]-like program. Hatfill chairs the Asymmetrical Biodiversity Studies and Observation Group (ABSOG) in [[Malaysia]], a not-for-profit trust he has established to support his [[drug discovery]] boat mission. Hatfill has also established Templar Associates II, a for-profit corporation in Puerto Rico as a revenue-generator and as an "environmental testing ground for new tactics, techniques, equipment, and procedures for ABSOG's designated mission as well as for the U.S. military".<ref name=Bird2014 />
 
Hatfill is also the medical director of EFP Tactical Medical Group, a London-based company that provides integrated training, security and tactical medical support services to government agencies, private corporations, and [[NGO]]s worldwide. (EFP Tacmed has extensive Middle Eastern and African contracts; it operates a remote jungle-training facility to test new equipment in "high-biodiversity areas".) He is also a board member of [[Doctors for Disaster Preparedness]], a politically conservative Arizona-based non-profit<ref name="21 days"/> described by some journalists as a "political fringe group".<ref name=guardian>{{cite news | last=Hickman | first = Leo | date=June 4, 2010 | url=https://www.theguardian.com/environment/blog/2010/jun/04/climate-sceptics-fringe-political-groups | title=Climate sceptics and fringe political groups are an unhealthy cocktail | newspaper=[[The Guardian]]}}</ref> He claims status as a fellow of the [[Explorers Club]].
 
In 2014, Hatfill publicly criticized the response of U.S. public health authorities to the [[Ebola virus epidemic in West Africa]] and suggested that it is possible that Ebola could be transmitted by [[aerosol]], an assertion which other experts have disputed;<ref>Hamblin, ''[[Op. cit.]]''</ref> his views on this have been characterized as misrepresentations of the primary scientific literature by other experts.<ref name="assessing the"/>

In November 2019, Hatfill and two other authors self-published ''Three Seconds Until Midnight''. The book examines current preparedness and unpreparedness for a devastating future influenza pandemic.<ref>Hatfill, Steven J., Robert J. Coullahan and John J. Walsh, Jr (2019), ''Three Seconds Until Midnight''; Asymmetric Biodiversity Studies and Observation Group, 932 pp.</ref>

===2020s===
In 2020, during the [[COVID-19 pandemic in the United States|COVID-19 pandemic]], Hatfill was interviewed on several right-wing media outlets including [[Stephen Bannon]]'s ''War Room: Pandemic'',<ref>[[Media Matters]] Staff (14 February 2020), [https://www.mediamatters.org/steve-bannon/virologist-tells-steve-bannon-his-coronavirus-conspiracy-theory-theory-crackpot "Virologist tells Steve Bannon his coronavirus conspiracy theory is from 'crackpot websites' and is a 'load of crap' "]</ref> ''[[The Epoch Times]]'', and [[Sinclair Broadcast Group]]'s ''[[Full Measure with Sharyl Attkisson]]''.<ref>Sharyl Attkisson (May 31, 2020), [https://sharylattkisson.com/2020/05/watch-pandemic-readiness/ "WATCH: Pandemic readiness and Dr. Steven Hatfill"]</ref>  He opposed the U.S. response to the pandemic, particularly the exclusion of [[hydroxychloroquine]] for early treatment of COVID-19, making unproven claims that the low fatality rate experienced by some nations is the result of their early use of the drug.<ref>{{Cite web|title=An Effective COVID Treatment the Media Continues to Besmirch {{!}} RealClearPolitics|url=https://www.realclearpolitics.com/articles/2020/08/04/an_effective_covid_treatment_the_media_continues_to_besmirch_143875.html|access-date=2020-08-05|website=www.realclearpolitics.com}}</ref>

In February 2020, Hatfill became an unpaid advisor to White House trade director [[Peter Navarro]] on the subject of the coronavirus pandemic. He interacted directly with senior officials at the [[Department of Health and Human Services]] (HHS), the [[Food and Drug Administration]] (FDA), and the White House, and he represented the administration in dealings with health care companies. Early in the pandemic he urged Navarro to quickly acquire tests and supplies, although he said such supplies should come only from U.S. sources. In an email to White House chief of staff [[Mark Meadows]] he said the president was being "grossly misadvised" by the White House Coronavirus Task Force, and recommended that the virus should be fought by widespread proactive administration of hydroxychloroquine, a malaria drug which the FDA had declared ineffective and potentially harmful to use for coronavirus.<ref name = "Diamond">{{cite news|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/health/2021/09/23/trump-election-challenge-covid-response/|title=Trump's election challenges distracted from covid response, White House adviser told colleagues|last=Diamond|first=Dan|date=September 23, 2021|newspaper=The Washington Post|access-date=October 28, 2025|url-access=limited|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220817163634/https://www.washingtonpost.com/health/2021/09/23/trump-election-challenge-covid-response/|archive-date=August 17, 2022}}</ref><ref name=":12">{{Cite web |date=|title=FDA cautions against use of hydroxychloroquine or chloroquine for COVID-19 outside of the hospital setting or a clinical trial due to risk of heart rhythm problems|url=https://www.covid19treatmentguidelines.nih.gov/antiviral-therapy/chloroquine-or-hydroxychloroquine-with-or-without-azithromycin/|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200828170647/https://www.covid19treatmentguidelines.nih.gov/antiviral-therapy/chloroquine-or-hydroxychloroquine-with-or-without-azithromycin/|url-status=dead|archive-date=August 28, 2020|access-date=2021-02-14|website=COVID-19 Treatment Guidelines|publisher=[[National Institutes of Health]]}}</ref> He repeatedly attacked [[Anthony Fauci]] and FDA commissioner [[Stephen Hahn]], at one point telling Fauci that he was "full of crap". Although the two were not removed from the task force as he urged, they were increasingly sidelined by [[Donald Trump]].<ref name = "Diamond"/>

Following the [[2020 United States elections|November 2020 election]], Hatfill became an active participant in Trump's efforts to [[attempts to overturn the 2020 United States presidential election|overturn the election results]], flying to Arizona to help challenge its election results, writing proposals for "Trump's Legal Fight", and sharing anti-Biden rumors.<ref name = "Diamond"/> According to House Majority Whip [[James E. Clyburn]] (D-S.C.) who chairs the [[United States House Select Oversight Subcommittee on the Coronavirus Crisis|House Select subcommittee investigating the COVID-19 crisis]], "Dr. Hatfill has refused to provide documents and misleadingly downplayed his involvement in the pandemic response in communications with Select Subcommittee staff".<ref>Diamond, ''[[Op. cit.]]''</ref>

In May 2025, it was announced that Hatfill had been hired by the second Trump administration as a senior HHS advisor in the [[Administration for Strategic Preparedness and Response]]. In an interview with the ''Washington Post'', he said he would be working to prepare for future pandemics. Hatfill also reiterated his belief that hydroxychloroquine was safe and effective for COVID, contrary to evidence showing that it does not work and may cause harm.<ref name="sun-2025">{{cite news |last1=Sun |first1=Lena H. |last2=Rein |first2=Lisa |last3=Johnson |first3=Carolyn Y.|title=Scientist who was part of covid treatment controversy returns to HHS |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/politics/2025/05/04/hatfill-covid-hydroxychloroquine-anthrax/ |access-date=5 May 2025 |newspaper=The Washington Post |date=May 4, 2025|url-access=limited}}</ref>

On October 28, 2025, the New York Times reported that Hatfill had been fired from his position as a senior adviser at the Department of Health and Human Services.<ref name="Stolberg"/>
